query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Elevated-temperature exposure in oxidizing environments triggers preferential oxidation of the active elements (Al and Ti) at grain boundaries in the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA, leading to the formation of continuous brittle oxide films that concentrate stress and promote intergranular crack initiation and rapid, catastrophic failure. In reducing atmospheres, the oxidation is suppressed, although internal segregation‐induced phase instability may still contribute to degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured, as-built HEA with a single-phase FCC matrix featuring a uniform microstructure and minimal pre-existing grain boundary oxidation or elemental segregation.
generation.intervention: Expose identical samples to controlled elevated-temperature conditions (e.g., 700°C) under contrasting gas environments – one set in an oxidizing atmosphere (ambient air with standard oxygen partial pressure) and another set in a reducing or inert atmosphere (purged with nitrogen or forming gas).
generation.conditions: Temperature range of approximately 600–800°C, exposure durations on the order of 100 hours, and well-controlled gas atmospheres to systematically vary the oxygen partial pressure.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and segregation of Al-/Ti-rich oxide precipitates along grain boundaries that weaken intergranular cohesion.
generation.mechanism: High-temperature exposure accelerates oxidation reactions at the high-energy grain boundaries; Al and Ti preferentially oxidize to form continuous, brittle oxide films that act as stress concentrators, thereby promoting intergranular cracking. Under reducing conditions, the diminished oxide formation should delay or modify the degradation pathway, although internal elemental segregation may still occur.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples in an oxidizing environment will show significant grain boundary oxidation, increased brittleness, and lower ductility relative to the as-built baseline, leading to early catastrophic failure under load. In contrast, samples exposed to a reducing or inert atmosphere will exhibit fewer or thinner oxide layers and improved retention of mechanical properties, although some internal degradation may be detectable.
generation.baseline: The as-manufactured HEA exhibits a uniform FCC microstructure with minimal segregation or oxide-related defects and high ductility/toughness.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies for service temperatures in the range of 600–800°C under environments with variable oxygen partial pressure; deviations outside this range may activate different degradation mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of selective oxidation and the interplay with any concurrent diffusion-induced elemental segregation remain to be quantitatively determined. Additionally, the extent to which reducing conditions can mitigate internal degradation (apart from oxidation) is not fully constrained.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical samples of the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA and subject them to identical thermal exposure (e.g., 700°C for 100 hours) in two distinct atmospheres: one oxidizing (ambient air) and one reducing (high-purity nitrogen or forming gas). Post-exposure, the samples will be characterized via high-resolution TEM/EDS to quantify oxide layer formation at grain boundaries and via mechanical testing (e.g., microhardness, ductility, fracture toughness tests) to assess embrittlement and degradation.
measurements: Thickness and continuity of oxide scales along grain boundaries (using TEM/EDS)
Changes in grain boundary chemistry (via EDS line scans)
Mechanical property degradation (ductility, fracture toughness, and microhardness)
Crack initiation and propagation patterns (using fractography)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidizing atmosphere does not lead to a statistically significant increase in grain boundary oxide formation and corresponding embrittlement (relative to the baseline and to the reducing atmosphere samples), or if the mechanical properties do not degrade as predicted, then the hypothesis that selective grain boundary oxidation is the dominant degradation mechanism and trigger for catastrophic failure would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The present work discovers the unique deformation behavior of a refractory high-entropy alloy at elevated temperatures.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as equimolar or nonequimolar single- and multiphase solid solutions, depending on the number and type of principal/secondary metallic elements with the configurational entropy greater than 1.61 R , (where R is the gas constant) ( [1] , [2] ). The minimization of the Gibbs free energy by increasing the configurational entropy results in the formation of a single- or multiphase solid solution, such as body-centered cubic (BCC) ( [3] ), face-centered cubic (FCC) ( [4] ), and/or hexagonal close-packed solid-solution phases ( [5] ) instead of intermetallic compounds ( [6] ). Moreover, the random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii leads to a severely distorted lattice with variations in the interatomic distances along the crystallographic direction of the unit cells ( [3] ). These features, in turn, contribute to desirable mechanical properties, such as high hardness, strength, ductility, and softening resistance at room temperature (RT) and elevated temperatures ( [3] ).

The classical “temper embrittlement” phenomenon [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ] —documented for over a century in conventional steels and other alloys—occurs upon exposure to specific temperature ranges, sharply reducing toughness and endangering engineering safety in critical applications such as aerospace, shipping, and petrochemical systems. [ [8] , [9] , [10] ] Temper embrittlement degradation is primarily attributed to the segregation of embrittling elements or the precipitation of brittle phases along grain boundaries (GBs), which act as stress concentrators and crack initiation sites, ultimately inducing brittle fracture under stress. Ductile−Brittle Transition

Our results demonstrate that aging the AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 alloy at 600 °C induces a ductile−brittle transition, which is different from the general degradation mechanisms—such as phase transformation, grain coarsening, or GBs embrittlement—commonly observed in conventional alloys when suffering heat treatment. [ [61] , [62] , [63] ] Instead, the transition originates from the coupled evolutions of LCOs and the B2/FCC(L1 2 ) PBs.

In the 600A alloy, the higher‐density and smaller‐sized L1 2 domains present perfectly ordered Ni 3 Al structure, exhibiting elevated APBE and elastic modulus (Figure 3 ), which raises the critical shear stress for dislocation motion. [ [64] ] Although these ordered domains notably harden the FCC(L1 2 ) matrix via both ordering and modulus strengthening (Figure S12 and Note S1 , Supporting Information), they simultaneously enhance the brittleness by impeding dislocation motion and concentrating stress. [ [65] , [66] , [67] ] Moreover, the ordered L1 2 generally promotes planar dislocation slip through a “glide plane softening” effect ( Figure 5 C ), whereby dislocations successively cut through and degrade the ordered regions, reduc

In summary, our study deciphers an unusual ductile−brittle−ductile transition in a eutectic HEA, driven by the dynamic evolution of LCOs and PBs configurations. Enhanced LCOs and the formation of jagged PBs lead to brittleness, while controlling the order degree of LCOs and the formation of a ductile transition zone along the PBs recovers the ductility. This discovery highlights the critical role of nanoscale chemical heterogeneities and PBs in determining material behavior, challenging and expanding the traditional paradigm of thermal embrittlement. Although LCOs are generally beneficial for strength‐ductility synergy in HEAs, our findings reveal their dual role: excessive ordering induces brittleness, whereas controlled LCOs restore ductility, which further indicates the necessity of meticulous control of LCOs for better performance. We believe that the uncover of thermal evolution behavior of HEA will advance the high‐temperature application of the HEA family.
